stories.title: Batteries combine in Vermont to be the state’s biggest power plant
stories.summary: Vermont's biggest power plant isn't a plant at all — it's 10,000 home batteries stitched together into a virtual grid. During July's heat wave, it dispatched 90 megawatts and saved customers an estimated $6 million.
stories.extended_summary: Vermont's largest power source isn't a smokestack or a turbine — it's more than 10,000 batteries sitting in people's homes and garages. Green Mountain Power's virtual power plant now has 110 MW of capacity, and during July's heat wave it dispatched 90 megawatts, roughly equivalent to taking 50,000 homes off the grid. The move cut an estimated $6 million from customers' peak electricity costs. It's a glimpse of a future where the grid is distributed, nimble, and owned in part by the people it powers.

stories.summary: A Washington State farm buried soil moisture sensors in its fields — and went from watering four times a week to just three times all summer. Same crops, way less water, and a blueprint for farming in a hotter climate.
stories.extended_summary: Outback Farm at Western Washington University used to water four times a week. The sensors tell farmer Terri Kempton exactly when the rain actually reached the plant roots, no hole-digging required. As the Pacific Northwest shifts from steady drizzle to big storms and dry spells, that kind of precision matters more than ever. It's a small, practical fix with a big payoff: less guessing, less water, and a farm better prepared for a changing climate.

stories.title: Preserving wildlife DNA for the future: Interview with the Frozen Zoo’s Katie Heineman
stories.summary: At the San Diego Zoo's Frozen Zoo, DNA from animals and plants is cryopreserved at -196°C for the future. The payoff is already here: two Przewalski's horses — a species extinct in the wild since the 1960s — were cloned from DNA stored for 40 years, born to surrogate domestic horse moms.
stories.extended_summary: Two Przewalski's horses named Kurt and Ollie were born in Texas — not to their own kind, but to surrogate domestic horse mothers, cloned from DNA that had been sitting in liquid nitrogen at the San Diego Zoo for 40 years. Their species went extinct in the wild in the 1960s. The Frozen Zoo, the largest biodiversity bank on Earth, stores genetic material at -196°C as what conservation leader Katie Heineman calls 'an optimistic act' — saving DNA for a time when we've solved the threats facing nature. It's already paying off, and the team is racing to build capacity worldwide before more species slip away.

stories.summary: Land for solar farms is getting scarce, so developers are getting scrappy. One Illinois project squeezed 11 megawatts onto a 22-acre site wedged between subdivisions, power lines, train tracks, and a wetland — and it's a blueprint for the future.
stories.extended_summary: The 22-acre site in Elgin, Illinois had everything going against it: two residential subdivisions on either side, high-voltage power lines overhead, train tracks, and a wetland in the corner. Most developers would have walked away. Instead, Cultivate Power split the installation into two arrays, deployed a high-density racking system, and squeezed 11 megawatts of solar out of the awkward footprint. As community opposition and land competition push solar onto smaller and smaller parcels, this kind of creative problem-solving is shifting from novelty to necessity — proof that the energy transition will happen in the margins, not just the open desert.

stories.summary: After a decade of lobbying and a pay cut that pushed them to organize, Tucson's substitute teachers just became the first in Arizona — and among the first in the nation — to win a union contract. Nearly 900 subs now have codified rights and benefits.
stories.extended_summary: Dolores de Vera and Jerry Schuster started showing up to Tucson Unified School District board meetings in 2016, after subs 'essentially got a pay cut.' This week, the governing board unanimously approved a 30-page collective bargaining agreement — making TUSD the first district in Arizona, and one of the few in the country, to unionize its substitute teachers. For Schuster, a sub of 25+ years who insists students call him Mr. Schuster until they graduate, the contract means nearly 900 educators finally have rights and benefits written into law.

As Malan takes his first sabbatical since taking over the course, the Duck carries on the experiment: can AI make students better thinkers instead of lazier ones?

stories.summary: Terrified of driving across Michigan's 5-mile Mackinac Bridge? There's a program where a trained driver takes your car across while you ride shotgun — and it's been quietly running since the 1980s. Thousands have used it.
stories.extended_summary: The Mackinac Bridge stretches five miles across open water, 200 feet up, with grated lanes where you can see the waves directly below your tires. It paused during COVID and now costs about $10 — a small price for anyone whose knuckles go white at the toll booth. Walkers and bikers can catch a ride too.

stories.title: AI helped a man with ALS speak nearly two million words
stories.summary: A brain implant powered by AI helped a father with ALS speak nearly two million words over two years. Casey Harrell can now talk with his daughter, crack jokes, and keep working — in a digital version of his own voice.
stories.extended_summary: Casey Harrell had thoughts he wanted to share with his daughter — but ALS had made his speech nearly impossible to understand. Now, an experimental brain-computer interface developed by UC Davis researchers, paired with AI, translates his attempts to speak into words on a screen, then says them aloud in a digital version of his own voice, built from recordings made before the disease progressed. This isn't a lab demo: Harrell used the system at home for more than 3,800 hours over nearly two years, communicating over 183,000 sentences. For a father who could still think, joke, and love but couldn't be heard, the technology gave his voice back.

stories.title: AI is helping save eyesight before it is lost
stories.summary: AI is catching diabetic eye damage before patients even notice vision changes. A quick retinal scan during a regular diabetes visit can flag disease on the spot — no separate appointment needed. A Johns Hopkins study shows it's already working in pediatric clinics.
stories.extended_summary: You can see perfectly fine and still have damage silently building at the back of your eye. That's the terrifying reality for people with diabetes — and by the time vision changes show up, the window to intervene may already be closing. AI is changing that. In some clinics, a staff member snaps photos of the retina during a routine diabetes visit, and an authorized AI system reads them on the spot. If something looks wrong, the care team arranges a specialist exam immediately. A randomized Johns Hopkins study of 164 young people with diabetes put the approach to the test. The software doesn't treat the eye — it just makes the first step impossible to skip.

stories.extended_summary: Jose Herrera was told his vision for outsourcing wouldn't work. Seven years later, his company Horatio has 3,500 employees, roughly 125 clients, and nine figures in annual revenue — all bootstrapped, zero outside capital. So he built dedicated teams in Latin America that function as true extensions of their clients, modeled more on a Silicon Valley campus than a traditional call center. In an era where AI was supposed to make call centers obsolete, Horatio is proving the human side still wins.

stories.summary: Minnesota's MINNCOR Industries has been putting incarcerated people to work since the 1870s — but the mission has changed. One instructor's 20-week printing course has become a pipeline to employment.
stories.extended_summary: Debra Woitalla has spent 18 years training incarcerated people in the print shop at Minnesota's Moose Lake facility. She's watched them produce everything from 'I Voted' stickers to DNR maps and brochures — and she's networked with printing industry contacts to learn exactly what skills employers want to see after release. That intel became a 20-week course on operating the facility's older offset press. It's one piece of MINNCOR Industries, which runs shops across six Minnesota correctional facilities teaching job skills in packaging, graphic design, printing, furniture and textile manufacturing, and — because this is the Land of 10,000 Lakes — dock and pier assembly. stories.summary: A Provo startup turned down investor money because the guy wanted them to make their kids' tablet more addictive. Instead, Scribbi's e-ink device treats a child's mistakes as data — quietly flagging patterns for parents without ever telling a kid they got it wrong.
stories.extended_summary: An investor sat across from Katarina and Keller Seamons with a simple pitch: make your kids' tablet more addictive and it'll be worth way more. They said no. That refusal is the whole point of Scribbi, the Provo startup's e-ink tablet built to be put down. When their daughter writes her S's backwards, most software would mark it wrong — Scribbi quietly flags the pattern for a parent and helps her fix it without ever telling her, in the moment, that she failed. It's a small design choice that flips the entire logic of kid-tech: a child's mistakes are information worth noticing, not noise for an algorithm to correct.

stories.title: CA Researchers Identify Odors That Repel Honeybees From Pesticides
stories.summary: UC Riverside researchers found chemical compounds that safely repel honeybees from pesticide-treated crops. Using a machine-learning model, they screened over 50 million compounds to find scents that push bees away — potentially saving pollinators from toxic exposure.
stories.extended_summary: Honeybees have over 200 odor receptors, which makes finding a scent that repels them — rather than attracts them — incredibly difficult. But that's exactly what researchers at UC Riverside just pulled off. Biologist Anandasankar Ray's team built a machine-learning model trained on chemical structures and real bee behavior, then screened more than 50 million compounds to find ones that safely push bees away from pesticide-treated crops. The goal isn't to harm bees — it's to redirect them, keeping them out of fields where pesticides could devastate their colonies. With pollinator populations in decline worldwide, a scent-based deterrent could be a genuine game-changer for agriculture and the bees that keep it running.

stories.title: CHECK IT OUT: The Wiyot Tribe Opened its New Affordable Youth Housing Complex Today
stories.summary: The Wiyot Tribe just cut the ribbon on 39 units of housing for young people who are homeless or close to it — built inside a former office building, a Victorian, and two new ADUs. Native youth get priority, and applications are already open.
stories.extended_summary: A two-story office building near the Samoa Bridge is now home. The Wiyot Tribe cut the ribbon on Jaroujiji Youth Housing, converting the old building into dozens of one- and two-bedroom units — plus a Victorian next door, two new accessory dwelling units, and a renamed house called Abalone House. In total, 39 units: 31 for permanent housing for 18-to-24-year-olds, seven for short-term shelter for 16-to-18-year-olds, and an apartment for the manager. Kitchens and living rooms are shared. Native youth are prioritized, but anyone who qualifies can apply — and Tribal Administrator Michelle Vassel says space will likely fill up fast.
